title: Verbs and affixes
goal: Use Malay prefixes and suffixes in the right places — a small, regular system that does the work English does with "-ed", "by", "for someone" and "have to".
bekal: know when Malay uses the affixed form of a verb and when the bare root
recognize the everyday verbs Malaysians actually use

dialogs.title: Dialogue — An assignment that's almost late
dialogs.intro: Saturday night in the college reading room. Sarah and Haziq are finishing an assignment that has to be handed in tomorrow morning.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Belum habis. Saya kena tulis dua muka surat lagi.
lines.id: Not yet. I still have to write two more pages.
lines.literal: not-yet finished. I must write two face letter more.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.id: When does it have to be handed in?

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Esok pukul sepuluh pagi. Kena muat naik kat portal.
lines.id: Tomorrow at ten in the morning. It has to be uploaded to the portal.
lines.literal: tomorrow o'clock ten morning. must load up at portal.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.id: If it's late, marks get deducted.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Saya tahu. Boleh awak semakkan sekejap?
lines.id: I know. Could you check it for me for a moment?
lines.literal: I know. can you check-kan moment?

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.id: Sure. Send it to my WhatsApp.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Dah hantar. Awak tengok bahagian kesimpulan tu.
lines.literal: already send. you look part conclusion that.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Hmm. Ayat ni panjang sangat. Cuba pendekkan.
lines.id: Hmm. This sentence is too long. Try shortening it.
lines.literal: hmm. sentence this long very. try short-kan.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.id: You're right. I'll fix it now.

lines.speaker: Haziq:
lines.text: Lepas tu simpan dalam PDF. Portal tak terima Word.
lines.id: Then save it as a PDF. The portal doesn't accept Word.
lines.literal: after that save in PDF. portal not accept Word.

lines.speaker: Sarah:
lines.text: Nasib baik awak beritahu. Terima kasih banyak!
lines.id: Lucky you told me. Thanks so much!
lines.literal: fate good you tell. receive love many!

notes: **Muka surat** ("face of the letter") = page. *Dua muka surat* = two pages. ⚠️ Malay *halaman* means a yard or garden (in Indonesian it means "page") — a trap that turns up in academic life.
**Hantar** means both **send** AND **take someone somewhere**. *Hantar tugasan* = hand in an assignment, *hantar saya balik* = take me home. Context decides.
**Markah** = marks, grades (from English *mark*). *Markah penuh* = full marks.
**Semak** = to check. *Semakkan* = check (for someone). You'll see it everywhere: *semak baki* (check balance), *semak keputusan* (check results).
**Ayat** means **sentence** — and also a verse of the Quran. *Ayat ni panjang sangat* = "this sentence is too long". Context tells them apart.

grammars.title: Affixes: a small kit that builds most words
body: Malay builds words by adding a few prefixes and suffixes to a root, the way English turns *write* into *writer* and *writing*. The system is regular, and the table covers what you need at A1. In everyday speech, many affixes are simply dropped — but you need to recognize them for reading.

head: Affix
Use
Malay examples
Note
rows: Often dropped in speech: *saya tulis*, *dia baca*.

after: ⚠️ **The suffix *-kan* is a hallmark of Malay.** It makes something happen ("make short" → *pendekkan* = shorten) or does something for someone: *betulkan* (correct, fix), *semakkan* (check for someone), *hantarkan*, *tolongkan*, *bukakan* (open for someone), *ambilkan* (fetch for someone), *belikan* (buy for someone). If you want one habit that quickly makes your sentences sound Malay, this is it.

⚠️ **Nouns in *-an* are very productive too:** *tugasan* (assignment), *jemputan* (invitation), *cadangan* (suggestion), *tempahan* (booking), *bayaran* (payment), *muatan* (load), *simpanan* (savings), *tuntutan* (claim). Find the root and you can often guess the meaning.

grammars.title: *Kena* — the passive people really use
body: Malay has a passive with *di-* (*ditulis* = is written), used fully in writing. But in conversation Malaysians far more often use **kena** ("get") — much like English "get" in "get fined", "get told off".
after: Note that *kena* carries **two loads at once**: passive and obligation. *Saya kena bayar* can mean "I got charged" — but "I have to pay" is far more common. Context separates them, and in practice it's rarely ambiguous.
⚠️ If you **don't** use *kena* in Malaysia, your sentences sound bookish. *Markah dipotong* is correct; *markah kena potong* is what people say.

blocks.text: Three that catch learners out: **siap** means **finished, ready** (*dah siap?* = done yet?), **ingat** means both "remember" and **think, assume** (*Saya ingat awak dah balik* = "I thought you'd gone home"), and **rosak** means broken. All three come up every day.

blocks.title: Commands and invitations
items: **Usah risau.** — Don't worry. (*usah* = no need, rather formal)

sections.title: Helper words: already, not yet, -ing, will

blocks.text: Malay verbs never change form for tense: *makan* is eat, ate, eaten and eating. Time is shown with small helper words placed before the verb — and spoken Malay has short Malaysian forms for most of them.

⚠️ **Tengah** as the "-ing" marker is one of the strongest signs of spoken Malaysian Malay. *Saya tengah makan* = "I'm eating". *Tengah* still also means "middle" (*tengah hari* = midday, *di tengah* = in the middle); position tells you which: before a verb = in the middle of doing it.

⚠️ **Lagi** has an extra meaning in Malay: **still**. *Dia lagi kat sana* = "he's still there". Elsewhere *lagi* means "more, again" (*satu lagi* = one more). (In Indonesian, *lagi* before a verb means "-ing" — so if you've met Indonesian, beware: a Malaysian saying *dia lagi kat rumah* means "she's still at home".)
